classification.difficultyReason: Find supplementary sine-rule candidates and reject the candidate incompatible with the given obtuse angle.

content.prompt: A triangle $ABC$ has $AB=6\text{ m}$, $AC=10\text{ m}$ and $\angle B=120^{\circ}$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the two candidate values of $\angle C$ given by the sine rule, correct to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\sin C}{6}&=\frac{\sin120^{\circ}}{10}\\\sin C&=\frac{6\sin120^{\circ}}{10}\\C_1&=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{6\sin120^{\circ}}{10}\right)\\C_2&=180^{\circ}-C_1\end{aligned}$$
To the nearest degree, the candidates are $31^{\circ}$ and $149^{\circ}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why there is only one solution for $\angle C$.

answer.short: The obtuse candidate and $120^{\circ}$ total more than $180^{\circ}$, so only $C\approx31^{\circ}$ is valid.
answer.worked: A triangle cannot have two obtuse angles. The obtuse candidate together with $B=120^{\circ}$ exceeds $180^{\circ}$, so it is invalid. The acute candidate satisfies $B+C<180^{\circ}$, leaving a positive third angle. Thus $C\approx31^{\circ}$ is the only solution.
